name: Power posing
statement: Holding an expansive, open posture for two minutes is said to raise testosterone, lower cortisol, increase risk-taking and make a person feel more powerful.
meaning: The claim is that posture runs the causal arrow backwards. Powerful animals and powerful people spread out; the hypothesis is that spreading out makes the body and mind behave as a powerful one does. Carney, Cuddy and Yap put four outcomes on that claim at once: a hormone of dominance, a hormone of stress, a gamble, and a self-report. The four are separable, and the fate of the idea turns on keeping them apart. A person can feel more powerful after standing tall without any of it showing up in saliva or in what they do next.

origin.who: Dana R. Carney, Amy J.C. Cuddy and Andy J. Yap
origin.note: Their paper is titled "Power posing: Brief nonverbal displays affect neuroendocrine levels and risk tolerance". Its abstract ends by claiming that two one-minute poses let a person "embody power and instantly become more powerful", with "real-world, actionable implications". Gronau and colleagues, writing in 2017, called the TED talk built on it the second most popular of all time.

evidence: Forty-two participants, 26 women and 16 men, were posed by an experimenter into two high-power or two low-power positions and held each for one minute. They were told the study was about electrode placement. Saliva was taken before the poses and about 17 minutes after. On testosterone the high-power group rose relative to the low-power group, F(1, 39) = 4.29, p < .05, r = .34. On cortisol it fell, F(1, 38) = 7.45, p < .02, r = .43. Offered $2 or a 50-50 die roll for $4, 86.36% of high-power posers gambled against 60% of low-power posers, chi-square(1, N = 42) = 3.86, p < .05, phi = .30. Asked how powerful and in charge they felt on a four-point scale, the high-power group averaged 2.57 against 1.83, F(1, 41) = 9.53, p < .01, r = .44.

replication.headline: Six preregistered studies put the feelings-of-power effect at 0.22, while the editors of the same set report virtually zero effect on any hormonal or behavioural measure.
replication.detail: Ranehill and colleagues tested 200 participants in 2015, 98 women and 102 men, holding each pose for three minutes with the experimenter blind to condition. Self-reported power replicated: a mean difference of 0.245 on the four-point scale, 95% confidence interval 0.044 to 0.446, t(193) = 2.399, p = .017, Cohen's d = 0.344. Nothing else did. Testosterone gave a mean difference of -4.077, 95% confidence interval -9.801 to 1.647, p = .162. Cortisol gave -0.028, 95% confidence interval -0.078 to 0.022, p = .272. Risk-taking in the gain domain gave -0.033, 95% confidence interval -0.085 to 0.019, p = .215. Two further behavioural tasks, risk in the loss domain and willingness to compete, also came out null. Comprehensive Results in Social Psychology then published seven preregistered studies in 2017. Preregistering the set rules out publication bias in advance, which Gronau and colleagues give as the first reason their analysis differs from earlier tallies. Six of the seven measured felt power, and Gronau and colleagues meta-analysed those 1,071 participants. Under a default prior their model-averaged estimate is 0.22, with a 95% highest density interval of 0.09 to 0.34 and a Bayes factor of 33.1 in favour of an effect. Under an informed prior it is 0.26, interval 0.14 to 0.37. Only one of the six studies was individually informative. The behavioural and hormonal side went the other way. The editors of the special issue list each of the seven studies failing its preregistered prediction, and write that there was virtually zero effect of power poses on any of the behavioural or hormonal measures. Ronay, Tybur, van Huijstee and Morssinkhof tested whether testosterone and overconfidence carry power posing through to risk-taking, and report in their abstract that they could not replicate the original findings and found no support for the extension. Gronau and colleagues state that their meta-analysis covered felt power only and did not consider behavioural or hormonal measures. Barel and colleagues posed 92 young adults in 2024 and found no difference between conditions on testosterone, cortisol, risk-taking or feelings of power. Within their high-power group a fall in cortisol predicted taking the gamble, b = -0.95, p = .011, which they call partial support for the original cortisol claim.

study.cite: Gronau, Q. F., van Erp, S., Heck, D. W., Cesario, J., Jonas, K. J., & Wagenmakers, E.-J. (2017). A Bayesian model-averaged meta-analysis of the power pose effect with informed and default priors: the case of felt power. Comprehensive Results in Social Psychology, 2(1), 123-138.

limits: No original effect size sits in the fields above. Carney, Cuddy and Yap report theirs as correlations without intervals, r = .44 for felt power, and a correlation cannot be set against the standardised mean difference the meta-analysis gives. The replicated figure carries no interval because the one Gronau and colleagues give is a Bayesian 95% highest density interval and putting it in a frequentist field would misdescribe it. The felt-power result weakens under one obvious test. Gronau and colleagues reran the meta-analysis on the 809 participants who said they did not know the effect, and the Bayes factor fell from 33.1 to 3.1, moderate rather than very strong. Most of the six studies had not excluded people who had seen the TED talk. That is the shape a demand characteristic makes, and the authors call it something future studies should explore. Taylor and Francis blocks automated access to its own copies of the special issue. The editorial was read instead from the accepted manuscript deposited at Queen's University Belfast, and the Ronay paper could not be read at all. Ronay and colleagues' conclusion above is quoted from their abstract, and their sample size is not stated here because it was not obtained. The published version of the Cuddy, Schultz and Fosse reply is also paywalled, so the p-curve figures below come from their accepted manuscript of 6 November 2017.
misreadings: The commonest error is to treat the whole idea as dead because Dana Carney says it is. Her undated statement is candid: the sample was tiny, subjects were run in chunks with the effect checked along the way, the risk-taking p-value of .052 from a Pearson chi-square was passed over for the .05 from a likelihood ratio, and the self-report question was chosen from many that were asked. She also names a confound nobody quotes. Participants were told at once whether they had won the gamble, winning is known to raise testosterone, and high-power posers gambled more, so the hormone result may be a winning effect. All of that is evidence about how the 2010 paper was produced. Her conclusion that the effect is not real is her judgement, and a co-author's confidence is not a datum. The second error runs the other way, treating the surviving felt-power effect as vindication of the original. It is not. The 2010 paper's claim was neuroendocrine, and no study on this page recovered the testosterone or cortisol result. The two claims have opposite fates and the words 'power posing' cover both. The third error reads the two p-curves as verdicts on the same evidence. Simmons and Simonsohn took the 33 studies Carney, Cuddy and Yap cited in 2015, dropped the two that examined only feelings of power, and curved the 24 p-values that survived their selection rules. That set showed no evidential value: neither test for right skew passed, half p = .11 and full p = .63, the curve was flatter than one from studies with 33% average power, p = .0016, and estimated average power was 5%, with a 90% confidence interval excluding anything above 14%. Cuddy, Schultz and Fosse added 21 studies to make 55 and put feelings of power back in. Their aggregate curve is right-skewed, half and full p both below .0001, with average power 44%. For feelings of power alone they report half p = .0009 and average power 58%. For the heterogeneous remainder left after the emotion and affect measures are taken out, right skew is marginal at half p = .0553 and absent at full p = .3601, and they call the support for evidential value very weak. The two analyses disagree about feelings and agree about everything else. The preregistered special issue is the reason the felt-power question does not rest on either. A last error is to assume the active ingredient is expanding. Elkjaer and colleagues pooled 73 studies in 2022 and found the difference sits with contractive displays against neutral ones, Hedges's g = 0.45, while expansive against neutral gave g = 0.06.
